primitives.name: Possession Event Tree
primitives.verbatim_quote: This is done by developing a probabilistic model of a basketball possession as a progression of events, where the probability of each event's occurrence is determined by the offensive players' skills, the defensive players' skills, and the complementarities between the skills of teammates.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'E_i': 'Event in possession progression (dimensionless)', 'S_o': 'Offensive skill vector (unitless)', 'S_d': 'Defensive skill vector (unitless)', 'C': 'Complementarity matrix (unitless)', 'f': 'Conditional probability function (dimensionless)', '\\gamma_{j_x}': "Player j's propensity for action x (probability)", '\\gamma_{k_x, def}': "Defender k's influence on action x (probability)", '\\beta_x': 'Own substitutability of action x (dimensionless)', 'X(E_i)': 'Set of parent actions to E_i (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Possession outcomes are Markovian; actions are conditionally independent given skill and complementarity states.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( \mathbf{S}_o \) or \( \mathbf{S}_d \) approach zero-dimensionality or \( \mathbf{C} \) becomes singular.

layer2.mapping: Maps player skill and complementarity to expected point generation through recursive event probabilities.

primitives.name: Substitutability Assessment
primitives.verbatim_quote: What separates this player evaluation scheme from previous ones1 is the focus here on identifying the substitutability between different game actions, and then using that to quantify the complementary effect teammates have on one another.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'\\beta_x': 'Own substitutability of action x (dimensionless)', '\\mathbb{P}(E_x)': 'Probability of action x occurring (probability)', '\\mathbb{P}(E_y)': 'Probability of alternative action y (probability)', '\\mathbf{S}_o': 'Offensive skill set (unitless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Substitutability is linear in action probabilities; fixed skill set across actions.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( \mathbb{P}(E_x) \) and \( \mathbb{P}(E_y) \) become non-differentiable or dependent.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to cross-correlation in signal processing, quantifying action redundancy.

primitives.name: Lineup Value Decomposition
primitives.verbatim_quote: This framework allows me to compute the value a player brings to a _particular_ lineup taking teammate spillovers into account, and allows me to assess which players help and hurt their teammates' production the most.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'V_j^{\\text{lineup}}': 'Value of player j in lineup (points)', 'Y_i': 'Statistical output of player i (points)', '\\mathbb{E}[Y_i | j]': 'Expected output of player i given presence of j (points)', '\\mathbb{E}[Y_i]': 'Baseline expected output of player i (points)', 'w_i': 'Weighting factor for player i (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Players' contributions are additive; baseline expectations are known.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When \( \mathbb{E}[Y_i | j] \) is undefined or \( w_i \) is non-positive.

layer2.mapping: Quantifies net teammate impact on lineup productivity via marginal expectation differences.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that NBA player evaluation must account for both individual skill and team synergy. The possession event tree models a sequence of actions as probabilistic nodes, where each node's outcome depends on player skills, defensive pressure, and teammate interactions. Substitutability captures how easily one action replaces another, informing how complementary skills interact. Lineup value decomposition isolates a player’s net impact on team performance by comparing conditional vs. unconditional expectations. These primitives form a dual system: one for predictive modeling (event tree) and one for evaluative attribution (value decomposition). Failure modes arise when skill sets are degenerate or when substitutability is misestimated. The framework avoids overfitting by conditioning on observed play-by-play data rather than arbitrary metrics.
